overview: Five documents trace the Japanese government's campaign from 1934 to 1936 to consolidate the rival Rengo Tsushin and Nippon Dempo news services into the state-favored Domei Tsushinsha, followed by a 1939 memorandum alleging that Domei was distributing fabricated reports abroad. Embassy despatches describe the financial and institutional mechanisms of consolidation, including Japan Broadcasting Company funding, government subsidies, preferential communications facilities, pressure upon newspapers, and a planned Cabinet information committee. Taken together, the file documents the replacement of competitive news gathering by a centralized system intended to shape domestic opinion, promote an officially approved image of Japan overseas, and reduce foreign influence.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the proposed amalgamation of Rengo and Nippon Dempo
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports government-backed negotiations to consolidate Japan's two leading news agencies as a means of tightening official control over domestic and international news.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Japan is pressing Rengo and Nippon Dempo (linked to AP and UP) to merge, officially for economy but actually to ensure only an approved viewpoint circulates ahead of an anticipated 1935-36 crisis; financing and leadership remain unresolved.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japan Broadcasting Company participation in the agency merger
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains a revised consolidation plan under which the Japan Broadcasting Company would finance the liquidation of the existing news agencies and join their successor.
subfiles.summary: Embassy reports the Japan Broadcasting Company joined the merger plan after the press refused a government loan; the broadcaster would finance liquidation using reserves and hold a lien, while nominally nonprofit, it monopolized radio under Communications Ministry control.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the establishment of Domei Tsushinsha
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Describes the organization, financing, political purpose, and competitive strategy of the new Domei Tsushinsha.
subfiles.summary: Domei Tsushinsha held its inaugural meeting on December 17, 1935, and planned to begin operations on January 1, 1936, under Tokichi Tanaka and Eisuke Fukuda. The Embassy regarded it as a strengthened and renamed Rengo, financed substantially by the Japan Broadcasting Company and designed to compel the unsubsidized Nippon Dempo to sell. Benjamin W. Fleisher warned that Nippon Dempo's disappearance would deprive the Japan Advertiser of an affordable, independent source of foreign news. The despatch also records military dissatisfaction that Domei was not sufficiently national or governmental, an ultimatum to Nippon Dempo, and the broader objective of unifying news services under government auspices.

subfiles.title: Despatch confirming the merger of Domei and Nippon Dempo
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Nippon Dempo's agreement to merge with Domei and reproduces the Japanese government's public rationale for a unified national news agency.
subfiles.summary: Minister Tanomogi announced Nippon Dempo-Domei merger effective around May 1936, framed as serving unified reporting and national policy; Grew instead sees government news control, plus plans for a Cabinet information committee spanning key ministries.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on fabricated Domei news
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Records Hornbeck's warning to the British Ambassador that Domei was intensively circulating fabricated reports about American and British policy.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck told Lothian that Domei reports contained false claims, including that Britain abandoned its Far East policy to help Japan impose peace on China; Lothian promised to relay the specific report.

interest: Shows how a Rengo-Nippon Dempo merger became state-controlled Domei, later seen spreading fabricated Japanese propaganda.
